transliteration_key.2: ء / ق (في اللهجة اللبنانية تُنطق همزة)

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Hello.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: Hi, how are you?

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Good, thank God. How are you?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: Fine, thank God.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: I'm Lina. And you?

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: My name is Rami.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: Nice to meet you, Rami.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Me too.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: I'm from Beirut. And you?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.arabic: أنا من صيدا، بس ساكنة ببيروت.
dialogue.transliteration: ana min Sayda, bas sakne b-Beyrout.
dialogue.english: I'm from Sidon, but I live in Beirut.

pair.english: Where are you from? (to a woman)

lessons.culture: In Beirut people often mix greetings, so "hi, keefak" and "marhaba" both sound completely normal, and friends kiss on the cheek. Asking "where are you from?" is a very common way to start a chat, because most families name a village or town of origin even if they live in the city.

exercises.prompt: A man says to you: "مرحبا". Reply naturally.

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but far too elaborate for a casual hello. Friends and shop staff say "marhaba" and get "marhabteen" back.

exercises.tip: "مرحبتين" literally means "two hellos": you return the greeting doubled.

exercises.prompt: A woman asks you: "كيفِك؟". Say you are well.

too_formal.feedback: The meaning is fine, but it sounds like a textbook. Lebanese say "mnee7, el-7amdella" in daily speech.

exercises.tip: A woman says "منيحة", a man says "منيح".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "_____ رامي." Meaning: My name is Rami.

too_formal.feedback: Grammatical but stiff. The spoken pattern is just "esmi" plus the name.

exercises.tip: "اسمي + name" is the whole pattern.

exercises.prompt: Translate into Lebanese Arabic: "What's your name?" (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: Understandable, but "ma ismuka" style is written or news Arabic. Lebanese say "shoo esmak?".

exercises.tip: "شو" (shoo) is the everyday Lebanese "what".

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means "Where are you from?" to a woman?

too_formal.feedback: Correct but formal and specific. The everyday question is "mneen inti?".

exercises.tip: Feminine ends in the "i" sound: inti, keefik, esmik.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Nice to meet you."

too_formal.feedback: That is written, formal Arabic. In conversation people say "tsharrafna".

exercises.tip: "تشرفنا" is said by both people when they meet.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "تشرفنا". Give a natural reply.

too_formal.feedback: Far too elaborate for a first meeting.

exercises.tip: "w ana kamaan" is the simplest reply.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in order: "اسمك / شو".

too_formal.feedback: Formal. The spoken question starts with "shoo".

exercises.tip: Question word first: "شو + اسمك".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I'm from Beirut."

too_formal.feedback: Correct, but adding "city of" is unnecessary and formal.

exercises.tip: "ana min + place" works for any city or village.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "أنا من صيدا، _____ ساكنة ببيروت." Meaning: I'm from Sidon, but I live in Beirut.

too_formal.feedback: Grammatical but bookish. The spoken "but" is "bas".

exercises.tip: "بس" also means "only" and "just", depending on the sentence.

exercises.prompt: A woman asks you how you are. Which is the correct question form for a woman?

too_formal.feedback: Correct and polite, but formal. Everyday Lebanese is "keefik?".

exercises.tip: Only the final vowel changes: keefak (to a man), keefik (to a woman).

exercises.prompt: Someone says "أهلا". Answer with the warm reply.

too_formal.feedback: Correct but written in style. Speakers say "ahleen" or "ahla w sahla".

exercises.tip: "أهلين" is warmer than a plain "أهلا".

reply.english: With pleasure (lit. may your eye be honoured).

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: Excuse me, can you help me?

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.arabic: إي، أكيد. أنا نور، شو بدك؟
dialogue.transliteration: ee, akeed. ana Noor, shoo baddak?
dialogue.english: Yes, of course. I'm Nour, what do you need?

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: I want some water, is that possible?

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: Sure, with pleasure. Here you go.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: Thank you very much.

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: You're welcome. Do you want anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.arabic: لأ، شكرا. آسف، ما فهمت الاسم.
dialogue.transliteration: la2, shukran. aasef, ma fhemt el-esem.
dialogue.english: No, thanks. Sorry, I didn't catch the name.

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: No problem, my name is Nour.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: Nice to meet you, Nour.

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.arabic: الشرف إلي. فيني ساعدك بشي تاني؟
dialogue.transliteration: esh-sharaf eli. feeni saa3dak b-shi taani?
dialogue.english: The pleasure is mine. Can I help you with anything else?

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: No, you're very kind. Thanks.

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: You're welcome any time.

pair.english: Excuse me, can you help me?
I want some water, is that possible?

lessons.culture: Beirutis sprinkle "merci" and sometimes "sorry" into Arabic without thinking, so "mersi ktiir" is as normal as "shukran". "Tekram 3eenak" is a warm way to accept a request, and being generous when someone asks for help or a glass of water is a point of pride.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "آسف!" after bumping into you. Reply.

too_formal.feedback: That is textbook wording. Just say "ma3leesh".

exercises.tip: "معليش" works for "it's okay", "never mind" and "sorry".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Thank you very much."

too_formal.feedback: Very formal. Speakers say "mersi ktiir" or "shukran ktiir".

exercises.tip: "كتير" (ktiir) means "a lot" or "very".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Excuse me" (to a woman).

too_formal.feedback: Formal and written. "law sama7ti" is what you say to get someone's attention.

exercises.tip: Add "i" at the end for a woman: sama7t / sama7ti.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "مرسي كتير". Reply.

too_formal.feedback: Correct but bookish. "3afwan" or "walaw" is what is really said.

exercises.tip: "ولو" (walaw) means "of course, don't mention it".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I want some water."

too_formal.feedback: That is Modern Standard Arabic. In Lebanese, "baddi" is "I want" and water is "mayy".

exercises.tip: "بدّ" + ending shows who wants: baddi, baddak, baddik.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "_____ تساعدني؟" Meaning: Can you help me? (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: Correct in writing. The spoken "can you" is "feek".

exercises.tip: "فيك" is "you can" (m), "فيكي" (f).

exercises.prompt: Which one is said by a woman apologising?

too_formal.feedback: A formal apology. "aasfe" is enough in daily life.

exercises.tip: The woman's form ends in "e": aasfe.

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "فيك تساعدني؟". Say yes, with a warm phrase.

too_formal.feedback: It is fine but formal. "tekram 3eenak" is common and warm.

exercises.tip: "أكيد" (akeed) is the quick, everyday yes.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in order: "مي / بدي".

too_formal.feedback: Written Arabic, not spoken.

exercises.tip: The verb-like word comes first: baddi + thing.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "آسف، ما _____." Meaning: Sorry, I didn't understand.

too_formal.feedback: Correct in writing. Speech uses "ma fhemt".

exercises.tip: "ما" plus past verb makes it negative: ma fhemt.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Is it possible?" / "Can I?"

too_formal.feedback: Too wordy. Lebanese just say "mumken?".

exercises.tip: One word is enough when you point at what you want.

exercises.prompt: You want to say "Yes, of course." Which is right?

too_formal.feedback: Correct but stiff. Speech uses "ee" for yes.

exercises.tip: "إي" (ee) is the Lebanese yes; "لأ" (la2) is no.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: What time is it now?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: It's one o'clock.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Really? I thought it was two.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.arabic: لأ، لسا وحدة. ليش، عندك موعد؟
dialogue.english: No, it's still one. Why, do you have an appointment?

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Yes, tomorrow at two.

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: And today I have five meetings.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: Five? Goodness!

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: Yes, but tomorrow I'm free.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: So, will we see you tomorrow?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: God willing, I'll see you tomorrow.

dialogue.speaker: Rami
dialogue.english: What time do you want to come?

dialogue.speaker: Lina
dialogue.english: At three. Okay, see you.

lessons.culture: Plans are almost always followed by "in shaa Allah", and Christian Lebanese say it too as an ordinary habit of speech. Casual plans are relaxed, so "bukra" (tomorrow) can be loose unless an hour is named.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "What time is it?"

too_formal.feedback: That is the standard Arabic question. Lebanese say "addeesh es-saa3a?".

exercises.tip: "قديش" (addeesh) means "how much"; put "الساعة" after it and it asks the time.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks: "قديش الساعة؟". It is one o'clock. Answer.

too_formal.feedback: Formal wording. Speech uses "wa7de".

exercises.tip: The number for time is feminine: وحدة, not واحد.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "It's two o'clock."

too_formal.feedback: This is the standard/written form. Speech says "tinteen" for two o'clock.

exercises.tip: Two o'clock is "tinteen", but the plain number two is "tneen".

exercises.prompt: Complete: "_____ منشوفك." Meaning: We'll see you tomorrow.

too_formal.feedback: Correct but formal. Speech uses "bukra".

exercises.tip: "بكرا" can go at the start or the end of a sentence.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "now"?

too_formal.feedback: Modern Standard, not spoken. Lebanese say "halla2".

exercises.tip: "هلق" (halla2) is the everyday Lebanese "now".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "I'll see you tomorrow." (to a man)

too_formal.feedback: Formal. The spoken future starts with "b-".

exercises.tip: "ب" plus the verb shows the plan: bshoofak, bektob.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in order: "بكرا / منشوفك".

too_formal.feedback: Formal. The spoken "we" starts with "m-".

exercises.tip: Both orders are natural in speech.

exercises.prompt: Which is the number three?

too_formal.feedback: The written form. Spoken has a "t" sound instead of "th".

exercises.tip: In Lebanese, ث usually becomes "t" (تلاتة, tlete).

exercises.prompt: A friend asks: "منشوفك بكرا؟". Say yes, God willing.

too_formal.feedback: It is fine but heavy. Speech shortens it.

exercises.tip: "إنشالله" (inshalla) is the fast spoken version.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Today."

too_formal.feedback: Unnatural filler.

exercises.tip: "اليوم" is used as it is.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "الساعة _____." Meaning: It's one o'clock.

too_formal.feedback: Formal spelling. Speech drops the middle letter: "wa7de".

exercises.tip: Hours use feminine numbers.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "How much?"

too_formal.feedback: Written or shop-window style. Speech says "addeesh?".

exercises.tip: Say it while pointing at the price.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: Excuse me, where is the market?

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: From here, walk straight.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: Is it far from here?

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: No, very close.

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: Then turn right at the bakery.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: Right, understood. And then?

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: You keep going and the market is there.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: Where is the nearest shop here?

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: On the left, after the pharmacy.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.arabic: آسف، ما فهمت. عاليمين ولّا عالشمال؟
dialogue.english: Sorry, I didn't understand. Right or left?

dialogue.speaker: Nour
dialogue.english: On the left, next to the bakery.

dialogue.speaker: Karim
dialogue.english: Thank you, may you have strength. Thanks a lot.

pair.english: Thank you, may you have strength.

lessons.culture: Beirut streets often have no visible names, so people give directions by landmarks such as a bakery, a pharmacy or a roundabout ("dawwar") rather than by street name. "Ya3Teek el-3aafye" is said to anyone who has helped you or is working, and the usual reply is "allah y3aafeek".

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Where is the market?"

too_formal.feedback: Standard Arabic. Lebanese use "ween".

exercises.tip: "وين" (ween) starts the question, like "where".

exercises.prompt: Which means "on the left"?

too_formal.feedback: The formal word "yasaar" is understood, but spoken Lebanese says "shmaal".

exercises.tip: "عاليمين" (right) and "عالشمال" (left) go together.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Turn right."

too_formal.feedback: Formal instruction wording. Speech says "leff".

exercises.tip: Add "i" to speak to a woman: leffi.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "من _____، امشي دغري." Meaning: From here, walk straight.

too_formal.feedback: Written form. Lebanese say "hoon".

exercises.tip: "من هون" = from here; "هونيك" = there.

exercises.prompt: Someone asks: "بعيد؟". It's close. Answer.

too_formal.feedback: Sounds like a textbook. Speech says "la2, 2reeb".

exercises.tip: "لأ" (la2) is the spoken no.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Turn left." (to a woman)

too_formal.feedback: Formal. Speech says "leffi 3a-shmaal".

exercises.tip: The woman's command ends with "i": leffi.

exercises.prompt: Which word means "straight ahead"?

too_formal.feedback: Written wording.

exercises.tip: "دغري" is spoken all over the Levant.

exercises.prompt: Put these words in order: "السوق / وين".

too_formal.feedback: Formal.

exercises.tip: Question word first.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Where is the nearest shop?"

too_formal.feedback: "matjar" is written Arabic. People say "ma7all" or "dekkaane".

exercises.tip: "أقرب" is "the nearest".

exercises.prompt: Someone says: "يعطيك العافية". Answer.

too_formal.feedback: Fine but plain. Lebanese answer with a blessing back.

exercises.tip: Say "الله يعافيك" to a man or a woman: allah y3aafeek.

exercises.prompt: Complete: "لف _____." Meaning: Turn right.

too_formal.feedback: Formal. Speech says "3al-yameen".

exercises.tip: "عا + اليمين" run together in speech.

exercises.prompt: Translate: "Straight on / directly."

too_formal.feedback: Written form. Speech says "3aT-Tool".

exercises.tip: "عالطول" also means "right away".

challenge.title: Your First Lebanese Conversation
challenge.instructions: Write and say a short Lebanese conversation of at least 10 lines. It must include a greeting, asking and answering names, asking where someone is from, one polite request, one thank-you exchange, one question about the time, and one set of directions. Use at least 8 target phrases from Unit 1 and include both a masculine-address form and a feminine-address form.
required_elements: A natural greeting using مرحبا, أهلا or أهلين.
A name question and a name answer.
A question using منين and a place answer.
A polite request using لو سمحت or لو سمحتي.
A response using إي، أكيد or a natural equivalent.
A thank-you exchange using مرسي or شكرا and عفوا.
A time question using قديش الساعة؟
A future plan using بكرا or a similar target expression.
At least two direction phrases such as عاليمين, عالشمال, دغري, هون or هونيك.

dialogue.speaker: Lina

dialogue.speaker: Samer

dialogue.speaker: Lina
